Q: Initializing very large C++ std::bitset at compile time A:

It's impossible to have a static constant std::bitset like that because:

  • There's no constexpr support for the constructor receiving const char*
  • VS 2013 is extremely old and doesn't even support constexpr. It only has partial C++11 support

Just check the compiled binary, your code definitely doesn't result in a single read-only compile-time object and must be computed at run time. But why use an ancient compiler? C++11 is practically the minimum version with useful features

So your at compile time requirement is out of the question, but in case construction at runtime is allowed then simply split the string literal into multiple smaller ones less than 2048 characters in case the total length is smaller than 65536:

ANSI compatibility requires a compiler to accept up to 509 characters in a string literal after concatenation. The maximum length of a string literal allowed in Microsoft C is approximately 2,048 bytes. However, if the string literal consists of parts enclosed in double quotation marks, the preprocessor concatenates the parts into a single string, and for each line concatenated, it adds an extra byte to the total number of bytes.

[...]

While an individual quoted string cannot be longer than 2048 bytes, a string literal of roughly 65535 bytes can be constructed by concatenating strings.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-language/maximum-string-length?view=msvc-160

As said, longer strings must be concatenated manually. Here

const int LENGTH = 1 << 16;
std::bitset<LENGTH> myBitset(
    "100101 ..."  // 2ᴺ bits
    "011001 ..."  // 2ᴺ bits
    ...
    "001011 ...", // must be one shorter than the previous lines: 2ᴺ⁻¹ bits
    LENGTH - 1    // size
);
myBitset[LENGTH - 1] = 1; // set the final bit

Alternatively just use an array instead of string literal:

static const char BITSET[LENGTH] = {
    '1', '0', '0', '1',...
    ...
    '0', '1', '0', '0'
};
std::bitset<LENGTH> myBitset(BITSET, sizeof(BITSET));

Q: Git - Staged Changes not showing in Android Studio A:

why does git's CLI indicate there is staged changes while Android Studio does not?

If git status says files are staged, they are definitely in the Git Index. Android Studio is just a visual wrapper.

If you prefer the way Git works in the terminal, go to Settings > Version Control > Git > Enable staging area. This syncs the IDE's behavior with the standard Git workflow.
